summary: After two iterations, the campaign has confirmed that hierarchical search finds near-optimal BLIS configurations 4.6× faster than random search at the high-load (rate=2000) regime, where the non-obvious winner (TP=4 with 2 replicas, batch=512) beats the naively expected single high-TP instance. The core hypothesis is validated, but two quantitative predictions were off, and NSGA-II's relative performance versus hierarchical remains ambiguous due to seed-dependent luck.
key_points: CONFIRMED: Hierarchical search reached 95% of optimal throughput (38,373 tok/s) in 14 evaluations vs. 64 for random search — a 4.6× speedup that exceeds the 3× success threshold. This held deterministically across all 3 seeds tested (CV = 0%).

SURPRISE — NSGA-II beat hierarchical at seed=42 (8 vs. 14 evals), but this is explained by lucky random warm-up sampling (≈19% chance per seed), not systematic superiority; expectation across seeds likely favors hierarchical.

PREDICTION ERRORS: Random search needed only 64 evals (not 150+) because the bundle undercounted qualifying configs (2.67% of space clears the 95% threshold, not 0.017%); and hierarchical was slowest in the easy low-load control (rate=50) because its fixed Phase 1 ordering evaluates the dominant TP=8/1 tier last.

STILL UNKNOWN: Whether hierarchical's advantage scales to larger budgets (1,000–2,000 evals), holds on different hardware (A100-SXM where the TP crossover rate differs), and whether NSGA-II systematically trails hierarchical in expectation over many seeds.

NEXT ITERATION should: (a) run all three strategies across ≥10 seeds to get reliable expected convergence curves, (b) test on A100-SXM to probe hardware portability of the TP=4/2 optimum, and (c) evaluate whether an adaptive Bayesian within-tier Phase 2 outperforms the current Latin Hypercube Sampling approach.
